judged.sentence: An elastomer is a type of polymer with viscoelasticity, meaning it exhibits both viscosity and elasticity, and is characterized by weak intermolecular forces, low Young's modulus, and high failure strain [1].
judged.chunk_text: An elastomer is a polymer with viscoelasticity (i.e. both viscosity and elasticity) and with weak intermolecular forces, generally low Young's modulus (E) and high failure strain compared with other materials. The term, a portmanteau of elastic polymer, is often used interchangeably with rubber, although the latter is preferred when referring to vulcanisates. Each of the monomers which link to form the polymer is usually a compound of several elements among carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and silicon. Rubber-like solids with elastic properties are called elastomers. Polymer chains are held together in these materials by relatively weak intermolecular bonds, which permit the polymers to stretch in response to macroscopic stresses. Elastomers are usually thermosets (requiring vulcanization) but may also be thermoplastic (see thermoplastic elastomer). The long polymer chains cross-link during curing (i.e., vulcanizing). The molecular structure of elastomers can be imagined as a 'spaghetti and meatball' structure, with the meatballs signifying cross-links. The elasticity is derived from the ability of the long chains to reconfigure themselves to distribute an applied stress.

Oleh karena itu, elastomer juga merupakan singkatan dari "elastic polymer" (polimer elastis). Elastomer merupakan polimer yang mempunyai sifat serta karakter seperti karet yang fleksibel dan elastis. Karet alam, karet sintetik butadiene rubber (SBR) serta karet silikon merupakan contoh dari elastomer. Pada kondisi normal, molekul materi elastomer membentuk semacam pilinan. Kemudian jika direntangkan, lilitan molekul terbentang, menjadi lurus, dan memanjang kearah gaya diberikan. Ketika elastomer dilepaskan, secara spontan, molekul akan kembali ke bentuk asalnya, yaitu untaian molekul yang terpilin dan terlilit. Each of the monomers which link to form the polymer is usually a compound of several elements among carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and silicon. Rubber-like solids with elastic properties are called elastomers. Polymer chains are held together in these materials by relatively weak intermolecular bonds, which permit the polymers to stretch in response to macroscopic stresses. Elastomers are usually thermosets (requiring vulcanization) but may also be thermoplastic (see thermoplastic elastomer). The long polymer chains cross-link during curing (i.e., vulcanizing). The molecular structure of elastomers can be imagined as a 'spaghetti and meatball' structure, with the meatballs signifying cross-links. The elasticity is derived from the ability of the long chains to reconfigure themselves to distribute an applied stress.

judged.chunk_text: Real-time Puncture Detection and Recovery for Pneumatic Soft Actuators. Soft robots offer safe and adaptive interaction with humans and unstructured environments through their inherent ability to deform and comply. Pneumatic actuators are one way to build soft robots. They are typically made from soft silicone materials and are especially effective for driving such systems, enabling smooth and adaptable motion. However, their compliant nature also makes them vulnerable to mechanical failures like punctures and tears, limiting practical deployment. To address this, we propose a puncture detection system for soft actuators using motion data from a single inertial measurement unit. Extracted features are used to train anomaly detectors for puncture detection and non-linear models to estimate severity. We also introduce a multi-chamber pneumatic soft bending actuator capable of diverse configurations via selective chamber inflation. Our algorithm identifies the punctured chamber and provides a severity score using a chamber perturbation scheme. Anomaly detectors are trained on normal operation data and detect damage through reconstruction errors, while severity is estimated by a separate model trained under slightly modified conditions. Finally, we demonstrate a failure recovery strategy to maintain actuation force post-failure.

judged.chunk_text: Soft Pneumatic Actuators for Soft Robotics: A Motion-Based Review of Actuation Mechanisms and Performance Trade-offs. Soft pneumatic actuators are widely used in soft robotics because they can produce large motions while remaining compliant enough to interact safely with objects, environments, and the human body. However, their performance is not solely determined by pressure. Instead, the response depends on the way the actuator is built, including the shape of its chambers, the placement of reinforcements, the use of folds, material stiffness, and the constraints that guide its deformation. As the literature has expanded, it has become more difficult to determine which mechanism is most suitable for a given application and which reported results can be compared across studies. This review examines soft pneumatic actuators according to the design strategies used to generate four motion classes: linear, bending, twisting, and omnidirectional actuation. For each class, it analyzes the structural features that define the deformation path, including braid angle, fold geometry, fiber orientation, chamber arrangement, structural asymmetry, and internal constraint layers.

judged.chunk_text: 3D printing, also called additive manufacturing, is the construction of a three-dimensional object from a CAD model or a digital 3D model. It can be done in a variety of processes in which material is deposited, joined or solidified under computer control, with the material being added together (e.g. plastics, liquids, or powder grains being fused), typically layer by layer. In the 1980s, 3D printing techniques were considered suitable only for the production of functional or aesthetic prototypes, and a more appropriate term for it at the time was rapid prototyping. As of 2019, the precision, repeatability, and material range of 3D printing have increased to the point that some 3D printing processes are considered viable as an industrial-production technology; in this context, the term additive manufacturing can be used synonymously with 3D printing. One of the key advantages of 3D printing is the ability to produce very complex shapes or geometries that would be otherwise infeasible to construct by hand, including hollow parts or parts with internal truss structures to reduce weight while creating less material waste. Fused deposition modeling (FDM), which uses a continuous filament of a thermoplastic material, is the most common 3D printing process in use as of 2020.

judged.chunk_text: Rotational Multi-material 3D Printing of Soft Robotic Matter with Asymmetrical Embedded Pneumatics. The rapid design and fabrication of soft robotic matter is of growing interest for shape morphing, actuation, and wearable devices. Here, we report a facile fabrication method for creating soft robotic materials with embedded pneumatics that exhibit programmable shape morphing behavior. Using rotational multi-material 3D printing, asymmetrical core-shell filaments composed of elastomeric shells and fugitive cores are patterned in 1D and 2D motifs. By precisely controlling the nozzle design, rotation rate, and print path, one can control the local orientation, shape, and cross-sectional area of the patterned fugitive core along each printed filament. Once the elastomeric matrix is cured, the fugitive cores are removed, leaving behind embedded conduits that facilitate pneumatic actuation. Using a connected Fermat spirals pathing approach, one can automatically generate desired print paths required for more complex soft robots, such as hand-inspired grippers. Our integrated design and printing approach enables one to rapidly build soft robotic matter that exhibits myriad shape morphing transitions on demand.

judged.sentence: Another method, additive manufacturing-facilitated blow molding (AM-BM), uses 3D-printed resin molds to produce thin-walled polymeric structures from thermoplastic materials, enabling the creation of flexible, compliant components [5].
judged.chunk_text: Additive Manufacturing-Facilitated Blow Molding for Functional Thin-Walled Polymeric Structures. Thin-walled structures capable of large, reversible deformation are key to multistable structures, origami, kirigami, and soft robotics. However, conventional fabrication techniques, including 3D printing, casting, and laser cutting, suffer from poor surface quality, low durability, complex processing steps, and restricted geometric freedom, hindering the repeatable production of thin-walled, continuous structures. Here, an additive manufacturing-facilitated blow molding (AM-BM) approach is introduced, combining the design flexibility of additive manufacturing with the robustness of blow molding. By replacing metal molds with 3D-printed resin ones, AM-BM enables rapid, low-cost fabrication of thin-walled polymeric components with tunable geometry and controllable wall thickness across diverse thermoplastic materials. The thickness control allows thin-walled components to function either as rigid load-bearing elements or as compliant hinges that permit reversible deformation.

judged.chunk_text: An elastomer is a polymer with viscoelasticity (i.e. both viscosity and elasticity) and with weak intermolecular forces, generally low Young's modulus (E) and high failure strain compared with other materials. The term, a portmanteau of elastic polymer, is often used interchangeably with rubber, although the latter is preferred when referring to vulcanisates. Each of the monomers which link to form the polymer is usually a compound of several elements among carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and silicon. Rubber-like solids with elastic properties are called elastomers. Polymer chains are held together in these materials by relatively weak intermolecular bonds, which permit the polymers to stretch in response to macroscopic stresses. Elastomers are usually thermosets (requiring vulcanization) but may also be thermoplastic (see thermoplastic elastomer). The long polymer chains cross-link during curing (i.e., vulcanizing). The molecular structure of elastomers can be imagined as a 'spaghetti and meatball' structure, with the meatballs signifying cross-links. The elasticity is derived from the ability of the long chains to reconfigure themselves to distribute an applied stress.

judged.chunk_text: Real-time Puncture Detection and Recovery for Pneumatic Soft Actuators. Soft robots offer safe and adaptive interaction with humans and unstructured environments through their inherent ability to deform and comply. Pneumatic actuators are one way to build soft robots. They are typically made from soft silicone materials and are especially effective for driving such systems, enabling smooth and adaptable motion. However, their compliant nature also makes them vulnerable to mechanical failures like punctures and tears, limiting practical deployment. To address this, we propose a puncture detection system for soft actuators using motion data from a single inertial measurement unit. Extracted features are used to train anomaly detectors for puncture detection and non-linear models to estimate severity. We also introduce a multi-chamber pneumatic soft bending actuator capable of diverse configurations via selective chamber inflation. Our algorithm identifies the punctured chamber and provides a severity score using a chamber perturbation scheme. Anomaly detectors are trained on normal operation data and detect damage through reconstruction errors, while severity is estimated by a separate model trained under slightly modified conditions. Finally, we demonstrate a failure recovery strategy to maintain actuation force post-failure.

judged.chunk_text: Soft Pneumatic Actuators for Soft Robotics: A Motion-Based Review of Actuation Mechanisms and Performance Trade-offs. Soft pneumatic actuators are widely used in soft robotics because they can produce large motions while remaining compliant enough to interact safely with objects, environments, and the human body. However, their performance is not solely determined by pressure. Instead, the response depends on the way the actuator is built, including the shape of its chambers, the placement of reinforcements, the use of folds, material stiffness, and the constraints that guide its deformation. As the literature has expanded, it has become more difficult to determine which mechanism is most suitable for a given application and which reported results can be compared across studies. This review examines soft pneumatic actuators according to the design strategies used to generate four motion classes: linear, bending, twisting, and omnidirectional actuation. For each class, it analyzes the structural features that define the deformation path, including braid angle, fold geometry, fiber orientation, chamber arrangement, structural asymmetry, and internal constraint layers.

One of the key advantages of 3D printing is the ability to produce very complex shapes or geometries that would be otherwise infeasible to construct by hand, including hollow parts or parts with internal truss structures to reduce weight while creating less material waste. Fused deposition modeling (FDM), which uses a continuous filament of a thermoplastic material, is the most common 3D printing process in use as of 2020.

judged.chunk_text: Towards end-to-end optimization in multimaterial 3D printing. Multimaterial 3D printing enables the fabrication of functionally graded components, but optimizing their spatial material distribution alongside structural topology remains a formidable challenge due to high-dimensional design spaces and complex constitutive modeling. This paper presents an end-to-end computational framework integrating sparsified physics-augmented neural networks with finite-element-based topology optimization. By extracting closed-form, composition-aware hyperelastic constitutive laws from experimental data, this approach facilitates exact symbolic differentiation via the adjoint state method implemented with FEniCSx, efficiently circumventing the bottlenecks of applying neural network constitutive models. This pipeline is deployed on soft robotic gripper applications, demonstrating continuous composition optimization for highly anisotropic contact responses, and the concurrent optimization of macroscopic topology and material distribution under non-failure stretch constraints. This methodology could replace laborious empirical prototyping, establishing interpretable machine-learning models as practical, robust design primitives for advanced multimaterial additive manufacturing.

judged.chunk_text: Elastomer ialah sejenis polimer yang bersifat kenyal atau kelikatkenyalan, iaitu suatu sifat yang ciri bagi getah. Ia boleh diubahkan bentuknya dan boleh ditarik hingga berganda-ganda panjangnya, tetapi balik kepada bentuk asal pula. Seperti gentian juga, ia mengandungi molekul-molekul yang panjang dan halus, dan menjadi teratur apabila ditarik. Tetapi selepas dilepaskan, ia berbalik kepada susunan rawak, tidak seperti gentian yang bakal teratur. Ini adalah kerana daya intermolekul dalam elastomer adalah lemah. Amnya, elastomer tidak mengandungi kumpulan-kumpulan berkutub yang membolehkan pembentukkan ikatan hidrogen. Ia juga tidak terdiri dari rantai-rantai yang boleh wujud dengan teratur untuk membentukkan daya Van der Waals. Walau bagaimanapun, elastomer berantai panjang harus mengandungi sebilangan kecil kaitan silang yang cukup untuk menahan rantai-rantai itu daripada ‘tergelincir’, tetapi tidak terlalu banyak sehinggakan rantai-rantai itu tidak boleh berbalik kepada keadaan rawak.

The approach opens new possibilities for force controlled, multifunctional magnetic soft robots for adaptive gripping, locomotion, and minimally invasive manipulation of biomedical tools.

judged.chunk_text: An elastomer is a polymer with viscoelasticity (i.e. both viscosity and elasticity) and with weak intermolecular forces, generally low Young's modulus (E) and high failure strain compared with other materials. The term, a portmanteau of elastic polymer, is often used interchangeably with rubber, although the latter is preferred when referring to vulcanisates. Each of the monomers which link to form the polymer is usually a compound of several elements among carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and silicon. Rubber-like solids with elastic properties are called elastomers. Polymer chains are held together in these materials by relatively weak intermolecular bonds, which permit the polymers to stretch in response to macroscopic stresses. Elastomers are usually thermosets (requiring vulcanization) but may also be thermoplastic (see thermoplastic elastomer). The long polymer chains cross-link during curing (i.e., vulcanizing). The molecular structure of elastomers can be imagined as a 'spaghetti and meatball' structure, with the meatballs signifying cross-links. The elasticity is derived from the ability of the long chains to reconfigure themselves to distribute an applied stress.

judged.chunk_text: Real-time Puncture Detection and Recovery for Pneumatic Soft Actuators. Soft robots offer safe and adaptive interaction with humans and unstructured environments through their inherent ability to deform and comply. Pneumatic actuators are one way to build soft robots. They are typically made from soft silicone materials and are especially effective for driving such systems, enabling smooth and adaptable motion. However, their compliant nature also makes them vulnerable to mechanical failures like punctures and tears, limiting practical deployment. To address this, we propose a puncture detection system for soft actuators using motion data from a single inertial measurement unit. Extracted features are used to train anomaly detectors for puncture detection and non-linear models to estimate severity. We also introduce a multi-chamber pneumatic soft bending actuator capable of diverse configurations via selective chamber inflation. Our algorithm identifies the punctured chamber and provides a severity score using a chamber perturbation scheme. Anomaly detectors are trained on normal operation data and detect damage through reconstruction errors, while severity is estimated by a separate model trained under slightly modified conditions. Finally, we demonstrate a failure recovery strategy to maintain actuation force post-failure.

Soft actuators have shown great advantages in compliance and morphology matched for manipulation of delicate objects and inspection in a confined space. This paper presents a magnet-based robotic skin that integrates a multilayer soft lattice with distributed Hall-effect sensor arrays and a tactile super-resolution model. External contact forces are converted to magnetic field changes by embedded permanent magnets, and the lattice spreads these changes across the sensing domain. This gives each sensor a large, overlapping receptive field and enables a large sensing area with minimal blind spots. Lattice parameters are tunable, enabling joint adjustment of mechanical compliance and transduction characteristics. Experiments validate localization accuracy and indicate scalability to larger surfaces, suggesting applicability to whole-body robotic skin and safe human-robot interaction.

judged.chunk_text: Automated design of soft-rigid hybrid robots for dynamic locomotion. Rigid-bodied robots often lack compliance needed to adapt to unstructured environments, while fully soft robots, though highly adaptable, struggle with scalability and load capacity. In nature, musculoskeletal systems balance strength and flexibility by integrating hard and soft tissues. Inspired by this principle, we present an automated design method for soft-rigid hybrids that optimizes a freeform soft-body shape, a stiff truss layout, and multi-channel actuation. Our differentiable simulator couples the material point method (MPM) for deformable bodies with extended position-based dynamics (XPBD) for truss elements, enabling gradient-based search. The optimization generates truss skeletons that transmit actuation forces to the soft body. We fabricate the optimized design and evaluate it on a walking task. Experiments reproduce the walking mode predicted by the optimization, which does not emerge without the skeleton. Modal analysis further suggests that the skeleton enables deformation modes near the actuation frequency that promote effective stride generation.

judged.chunk_text: 3D printing, also called additive manufacturing, is the construction of a three-dimensional object from a CAD model or a digital 3D model. It can be done in a variety of processes in which material is deposited, joined or solidified under computer control, with the material being added together (e.g. plastics, liquids, or powder grains being fused), typically layer by layer. In the 1980s, 3D printing techniques were considered suitable only for the production of functional or aesthetic prototypes, and a more appropriate term for it at the time was rapid prototyping. As of 2019, the precision, repeatability, and material range of 3D printing have increased to the point that some 3D printing processes are considered viable as an industrial-production technology; in this context, the term additive manufacturing can be used synonymously with 3D printing. One of the key advantages of 3D printing is the ability to produce very complex shapes or geometries that would be otherwise infeasible to construct by hand, including hollow parts or parts with internal truss structures to reduce weight while creating less material waste. Fused deposition modeling (FDM), which uses a continuous filament of a thermoplastic material, is the most common 3D printing process in use as of 2020.

judged.chunk_text: Rotational Multi-material 3D Printing of Soft Robotic Matter with Asymmetrical Embedded Pneumatics. The rapid design and fabrication of soft robotic matter is of growing interest for shape morphing, actuation, and wearable devices. Here, we report a facile fabrication method for creating soft robotic materials with embedded pneumatics that exhibit programmable shape morphing behavior. Using rotational multi-material 3D printing, asymmetrical core-shell filaments composed of elastomeric shells and fugitive cores are patterned in 1D and 2D motifs. By precisely controlling the nozzle design, rotation rate, and print path, one can control the local orientation, shape, and cross-sectional area of the patterned fugitive core along each printed filament. Once the elastomeric matrix is cured, the fugitive cores are removed, leaving behind embedded conduits that facilitate pneumatic actuation. Using a connected Fermat spirals pathing approach, one can automatically generate desired print paths required for more complex soft robots, such as hand-inspired grippers. Our integrated design and printing approach enables one to rapidly build soft robotic matter that exhibits myriad shape morphing transitions on demand.

judged.chunk_text: BactoBot: A Low-Cost, Bacteria-Inspired Soft Underwater Robot for Marine Exploration. Traditional rigid underwater vehicles pose risks to delicate marine ecosystems due to high-speed propellers and rigid hulls. This paper presents BactoBot, a low-cost, soft underwater robot designed for safe and gentle marine exploration. Inspired by the efficient flagellar propulsion of bacteria, BactoBot features 12 flexible, silicone-based arms arranged on a dodecahedral frame. Unlike high-cost research platforms, this prototype was fabricated using accessible DIY methods, including food-grade silicone molding, FDM 3D printing, and off-the-shelf DC motors. A novel multi-stage waterproofing protocol was developed to seal rotating shafts using a grease-filled chamber system, ensuring reliability at low cost. The robot was successfully tested in a controlled aquatic environment, demonstrating stable forward propulsion and turning maneuvers. Soft actuators have shown great advantages in compliance and morphology matched for manipulation of delicate objects and inspection in a confined space. There is an unmet need for a soft actuator that can provide torsional motion to e.g. enlarge working space and increase degrees of freedom. Towards this goal, we present origami-inspired soft pneumatic actuators (OSPAs) made from silicone. The prototype can output a rotation of more than one revolution (up to 435°), more significant than its counterparts. Its rotation ratio (=rotation angle/ aspect ratio) is more than 136°, about twice the largest one in other literature. We describe the design and fabrication method, build the analytical model and simulation model, and analyze and optimize the parameters. Finally, we demonstrate the potentially extensive utility of the OSPAs through their integration into a gripper capable of simultaneously grasping and lifting fragile or flat objects, a versatile robot arm capable of picking and placing items at the right angle with the twisting actuators, and a soft snake robot capable of changing attitude and directions by torsion of the twisting actuators.

judged.chunk_text: Rotational Multi-material 3D Printing of Soft Robotic Matter with Asymmetrical Embedded Pneumatics. The rapid design and fabrication of soft robotic matter is of growing interest for shape morphing, actuation, and wearable devices. Here, we report a facile fabrication method for creating soft robotic materials with embedded pneumatics that exhibit programmable shape morphing behavior. Using rotational multi-material 3D printing, asymmetrical core-shell filaments composed of elastomeric shells and fugitive cores are patterned in 1D and 2D motifs. By precisely controlling the nozzle design, rotation rate, and print path, one can control the local orientation, shape, and cross-sectional area of the patterned fugitive core along each printed filament. Once the elastomeric matrix is cured, the fugitive cores are removed, leaving behind embedded conduits that facilitate pneumatic actuation. Using a connected Fermat spirals pathing approach, one can automatically generate desired print paths required for more complex soft robots, such as hand-inspired grippers. Our integrated design and printing approach enables one to rapidly build soft robotic matter that exhibits myriad shape morphing transitions on demand.

judged.chunk_text: BactoBot: A Low-Cost, Bacteria-Inspired Soft Underwater Robot for Marine Exploration. Traditional rigid underwater vehicles pose risks to delicate marine ecosystems due to high-speed propellers and rigid hulls. This paper presents BactoBot, a low-cost, soft underwater robot designed for safe and gentle marine exploration. Inspired by the efficient flagellar propulsion of bacteria, BactoBot features 12 flexible, silicone-based arms arranged on a dodecahedral frame. Unlike high-cost research platforms, this prototype was fabricated using accessible DIY methods, including food-grade silicone molding, FDM 3D printing, and off-the-shelf DC motors. A novel multi-stage waterproofing protocol was developed to seal rotating shafts using a grease-filled chamber system, ensuring reliability at low cost. The robot was successfully tested in a controlled aquatic environment, demonstrating stable forward propulsion and turning maneuvers. With a total fabrication cost of approximately $355 USD, this project validates the feasibility of democratizing soft robotics for marine science in resource-constrained settings.

judged.chunk_text: One Print, Many Moves: Monolithic Origami-inspired Folding Actuator for Composable Soft Multi-DoF Systems. Conventional soft robot actuators excel in compliance, but their uncontrolled deformations compromise accuracy and hinder scaling to multi-degree-of-freedom (DoF) systems. We introduce a MONOlithic ORIGAMI-inspired soft folding actuator design (MONORIGAMI) that establishes a design strategy based on spatially programmed stiffness anisotropy to preserve material compliance along desired folding directions while selectively restricting deformation in unwanted directions. The actuator leverages stiffness tiers based on material thickness, patterned in an origami-inspired geometry with facets and creases, converting unconstrained soft deformation into accurate, repeatable, and composable folding motions without additional reinforcements. The design is fully 3D-printable through a single-material, single-print process that requires no assembly. Each actuator serves as a scalable motion primitive, and linking and orienting multiple actuators mechanically programs multi-DoF trajectories.

Due to these properties and its ease of manufacturing and shaping, silicone rubber can be found in a wide variety of products, including voltage line insulators; automotive applications; cooking, baking, and food storage products; apparel such as undergarments, sportswear, and footwear; electronics; medical devices and implants; and in home repair and hardware, in products such as silicone sealants. judged.chunk_text: An elastomer is a polymer with viscoelasticity (i.e. both viscosity and elasticity) and with weak intermolecular forces, generally low Young's modulus (E) and high failure strain compared with other materials. The term, a portmanteau of elastic polymer, is often used interchangeably with rubber, although the latter is preferred when referring to vulcanisates. Each of the monomers which link to form the polymer is usually a compound of several elements among carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and silicon. Rubber-like solids with elastic properties are called elastomers. Polymer chains are held together in these materials by relatively weak intermolecular bonds, which permit the polymers to stretch in response to macroscopic stresses. Elastomers are usually thermosets (requiring vulcanization) but may also be thermoplastic (see thermoplastic elastomer). The long polymer chains cross-link during curing (i.e., vulcanizing). The molecular structure of elastomers can be imagined as a 'spaghetti and meatball' structure, with the meatballs signifying cross-links. The elasticity is derived from the ability of the long chains to reconfigure themselves to distribute an applied stress.

judged.chunk_text: 3D printing, also called additive manufacturing, is the construction of a three-dimensional object from a CAD model or a digital 3D model. In the 1980s, 3D printing techniques were considered suitable only for the production of functional or aesthetic prototypes, and a more appropriate term for it at the time was rapid prototyping. As of 2019, the precision, repeatability, and material range of 3D printing have increased to the point that some 3D printing processes are considered viable as an industrial-production technology; in this context, the term additive manufacturing can be used synonymously with 3D printing. One of the key advantages of 3D printing is the ability to produce very complex shapes or geometries that would be otherwise infeasible to construct by hand, including hollow parts or parts with internal truss structures to reduce weight while creating less material waste. Fused deposition modeling (FDM), which uses a continuous filament of a thermoplastic material, is the most common 3D printing process in use as of 2020.

judged.chunk_text: Rotational Multi-material 3D Printing of Soft Robotic Matter with Asymmetrical Embedded Pneumatics. The rapid design and fabrication of soft robotic matter is of growing interest for shape morphing, actuation, and wearable devices. Here, we report a facile fabrication method for creating soft robotic materials with embedded pneumatics that exhibit programmable shape morphing behavior. Using rotational multi-material 3D printing, asymmetrical core-shell filaments composed of elastomeric shells and fugitive cores are patterned in 1D and 2D motifs. By precisely controlling the nozzle design, rotation rate, and print path, one can control the local orientation, shape, and cross-sectional area of the patterned fugitive core along each printed filament. Once the elastomeric matrix is cured, the fugitive cores are removed, leaving behind embedded conduits that facilitate pneumatic actuation. Using a connected Fermat spirals pathing approach, one can automatically generate desired print paths required for more complex soft robots, such as hand-inspired grippers. Our integrated design and printing approach enables one to rapidly build soft robotic matter that exhibits myriad shape morphing transitions on demand.

judged.chunk_text: 3D-printed Soft Optical sensor with a Lens (SOLen) for light guidance in mechanosensing. Additive manufacturing is enabling soft robots with increasingly complex geometries, creating a demand for sensing solutions that remain compatible with single-material, one-step fabrication. Here, we present an approach for 3D printed soft optical sensing (SOLen), in which a printed lens is placed in front of an emitter within a Y-shaped waveguide. judged.chunk_text: Origami-inspired soft twisting actuator. Soft actuators have shown great advantages in compliance and morphology matched for manipulation of delicate objects and inspection in a confined space. There is an unmet need for a soft actuator that can provide torsional motion to e.g. enlarge working space and increase degrees of freedom. Towards this goal, we present origami-inspired soft pneumatic actuators (OSPAs) made from silicone. The prototype can output a rotation of more than one revolution (up to 435°), more significant than its counterparts. Its rotation ratio (=rotation angle/ aspect ratio) is more than 136°, about twice the largest one in other literature. We describe the design and fabrication method, build the analytical model and simulation model, and analyze and optimize the parameters. Finally, we demonstrate the potentially extensive utility of the OSPAs through their integration into a gripper capable of simultaneously grasping and lifting fragile or flat objects, a versatile robot arm capable of picking and placing items at the right angle with the twisting actuators, and a soft snake robot capable of changing attitude and directions by torsion of the twisting actuators.

judged.chunk_text: Inchworm-Inspired Soft Robot with Groove-Guided Locomotion. Soft robots require directional control to navigate complex terrains. However, achieving such control often requires multiple actuators, which increases mechanical complexity, complicates control systems, and raises energy consumption. Here, we introduce an inchworm-inspired soft robot whose locomotion direction is controlled passively by patterned substrates. The robot employs a single rolled dielectric elastomer actuator, while groove patterns on a 3D-printed substrate guide its alignment and trajectory. Through systematic experiments, we demonstrate that varying groove angles enables precise control of locomotion direction without the need for complex actuation strategies. This groove-guided approach reduces energy consumption, simplifies robot design, and expands the applicability of bio-inspired soft robots in fields such as search and rescue, pipe inspection, and planetary exploration.

judged.chunk_text: Novel bio-inspired soft actuators for upper-limb exoskeletons: design, fabrication and feasibility study. Soft robots have been increasingly utilized as sophisticated tools in physical rehabilitation, particularly for assisting patients with neuromotor impairments. However, many soft robotics for rehabilitation applications are characterized by limitations such as slow response times, restricted range of motion, and low output force. There are also limited studies on the precise position and force control of wearable soft actuators. Furthermore, not many studies articulate how bellow-structured actuator designs quantitatively contribute to the robots' capability. This study introduces a paradigm of upper limb soft actuator design. This paradigm comprises two actuators: the Lobster-Inspired Silicone Pneumatic Robot (LISPER) for the elbow and the Scallop-Shaped Pneumatic Robot (SCASPER) for the shoulder. LISPER is characterized by higher bandwidth, increased output force/torque, and high linearity. SCASPER is characterized by high output force/torque and simplified fabrication processes.

judged.chunk_text: Electroadhesive Clutches for Programmable Shape Morphing of Soft Actuators. Soft robotic actuators are safe and adaptable devices with inherent compliance, which makes them attractive for manipulating delicate and complex objects. Researchers have integrated stiff materials into soft actuators to increase their force capacity and direct their deformation. However, these embedded materials have largely been pre-prescribed and static, which constrains the actuators to a predetermined range of motion. In this work, electroadhesive (EA) clutches integrated on a single-chamber soft pneumatic actuator (SPA) provide local programmable stiffness modulation to control the actuator deformation. We show that activating different clutch patterns inflates a silicone membrane into pyramidal, round, and plateau shapes. Curvatures from these shapes are combined during actuation to apply forces on both a 3.7 g and 820 g object along five different degrees of freedom (DoF). The actuator workspace is up to 12 mm for light objects. Clutch deactivation, which results in local elastomeric expansion, rapidly applies forces up to 3.2 N to an object resting on the surface and launches a 3.7 g object in controlled directions.

judged.chunk_text: 3D printing, also called additive manufacturing, is the construction of a three-dimensional object from a CAD model or a digital 3D model. It can be done in a variety of processes in which material is deposited, joined or solidified under computer control, with the material being added together (e.g. plastics, liquids, or powder grains being fused), typically layer by layer. In the 1980s, 3D printing techniques were considered suitable only for the production of functional or aesthetic prototypes, and a more appropriate term for it at the time was rapid prototyping. As of 2019, the precision, repeatability, and material range of 3D printing have increased to the point that some 3D printing processes are considered viable as an industrial-production technology; in this context, the term additive manufacturing can be used synonymously with 3D printing. One of the key advantages of 3D printing is the ability to produce very complex shapes or geometries that would be otherwise infeasible to construct by hand, including hollow parts or parts with internal truss structures to reduce weight while creating less material waste. Fused deposition modeling (FDM), which uses a continuous filament of a thermoplastic material, is the most common 3D printing process in use as of 2020.

judged.chunk_text: Rotational Multi-material 3D Printing of Soft Robotic Matter with Asymmetrical Embedded Pneumatics. The rapid design and fabrication of soft robotic matter is of growing interest for shape morphing, actuation, and wearable devices. Here, we report a facile fabrication method for creating soft robotic materials with embedded pneumatics that exhibit programmable shape morphing behavior. Using rotational multi-material 3D printing, asymmetrical core-shell filaments composed of elastomeric shells and fugitive cores are patterned in 1D and 2D motifs. By precisely controlling the nozzle design, rotation rate, and print path, one can control the local orientation, shape, and cross-sectional area of the patterned fugitive core along each printed filament. Once the elastomeric matrix is cured, the fugitive cores are removed, leaving behind embedded conduits that facilitate pneumatic actuation. Using a connected Fermat spirals pathing approach, one can automatically generate desired print paths required for more complex soft robots, such as hand-inspired grippers. Our integrated design and printing approach enables one to rapidly build soft robotic matter that exhibits myriad shape morphing transitions on demand.

judged.chunk_text: Inchworm-Inspired Soft Robot with Groove-Guided Locomotion. Soft robots require directional control to navigate complex terrains. However, achieving such control often requires multiple actuators, which increases mechanical complexity, complicates control systems, and raises energy consumption. Here, we introduce an inchworm-inspired soft robot whose locomotion direction is controlled passively by patterned substrates. The robot employs a single rolled dielectric elastomer actuator, while groove patterns on a 3D-printed substrate guide its alignment and trajectory. Through systematic experiments, we demonstrate that varying groove angles enables precise control of locomotion direction without the need for complex actuation strategies. This groove-guided approach reduces energy consumption, simplifies robot design, and expands the applicability of bio-inspired soft robots in fields such as search and rescue, pipe inspection, and planetary exploration.

The elasticity is derived from the ability of the long chains to reconfigure themselves to distribute an applied stress.

Karet alam, karet sintetik butadiene rubber (SBR) serta karet silikon merupakan contoh dari elastomer. Pada kondisi normal, molekul materi elastomer membentuk semacam pilinan. Ketika elastomer dilepaskan, secara spontan, molekul akan kembali ke bentuk asalnya, yaitu untaian molekul yang terpilin dan terlilit. Elastomer yang sejarah penggunaannya paling panjang adalah poli-isoprena. Karet alami masih merupakan polimer industri yang penting, akan tetapi saat ini polimer tersebut bersaing dengan polimer sintetik, seperti karet stirena-butadiena dan butadiena. Karet elastomer tersebut merupakan bahan sintetik yang berbahan dasar minyak bumi.

judged.chunk_text: 3D printing, also called additive manufacturing, is the construction of a three-dimensional object from a CAD model or a digital 3D model. In the 1980s, 3D printing techniques were considered suitable only for the production of functional or aesthetic prototypes, and a more appropriate term for it at the time was rapid prototyping. An elastomer is a polymer with viscoelasticity (i.e. both viscosity and elasticity) and with weak intermolecular forces, generally low Young's modulus (E) and high failure strain compared with other materials. The term, a portmanteau of elastic polymer, is often used interchangeably with rubber, although the latter is preferred when referring to vulcanisates. Each of the monomers which link to form the polymer is usually a compound of several elements among carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and silicon. Rubber-like solids with elastic properties are called elastomers. Polymer chains are held together in these materials by relatively weak intermolecular bonds, which permit the polymers to stretch in response to macroscopic stresses. Elastomers are usually thermosets (requiring vulcanization) but may also be thermoplastic (see thermoplastic elastomer). The long polymer chains cross-link during curing (i.e., vulcanizing). The molecular structure of elastomers can be imagined as a 'spaghetti and meatball' structure, with the meatballs signifying cross-links. The elasticity is derived from the ability of the long chains to reconfigure themselves to distribute an applied stress.

judged.chunk_text: FORTE: Tactile Force and Slip Sensing on Compliant Fingers for Delicate Manipulation. Handling fragile objects remains a major challenge for robotic manipulation. Tactile sensing and soft robotics can improve delicate object handling, but typically involve high integration complexity or slow response times. We address these issues through FORTE, an easy-to-fabricate tactile sensing system. FORTE uses 3D-printed fin-ray grippers with internal air channels to provide low-latency force and slip feedback. This feedback allows us to apply just enough force to grasp objects without damaging them. We accurately estimate grasping forces from 0-8 N with an average error of 0.2 N, and detect slip events within 100 ms of occurring. FORTE can grasp a wide range of slippery, fragile, and deformable objects, including raspberries and potato chips with 92% success and achieves 93% accuracy in detecting slip events. These results highlight FORTE's potential as a robust solution for delicate robotic manipulation. Project page: https://merge-lab.github.io/FORTE/

judged.sentence: Nimble robots, jaise ki FORTE ya origami-inspired soft actuators, aam taur par silicone, 3D-printed materials, aur pneumatic systems se bane hote hain [1], [2].
judged.chunk_text: Origami-inspired soft twisting actuator. Soft actuators have shown great advantages in compliance and morphology matched for manipulation of delicate objects and inspection in a confined space. There is an unmet need for a soft actuator that can provide torsional motion to e.g. enlarge working space and increase degrees of freedom. Towards this goal, we present origami-inspired soft pneumatic actuators (OSPAs) made from silicone. The prototype can output a rotation of more than one revolution (up to 435°), more significant than its counterparts. Its rotation ratio (=rotation angle/ aspect ratio) is more than 136°, about twice the largest one in other literature. We describe the design and fabrication method, build the analytical model and simulation model, and analyze and optimize the parameters. Finally, we demonstrate the potentially extensive utility of the OSPAs through their integration into a gripper capable of simultaneously grasping and lifting fragile or flat objects, a versatile robot arm capable of picking and placing items at the right angle with the twisting actuators, and a soft snake robot capable of changing attitude and directions by torsion of the twisting actuators.

judged.chunk_text: Magnet-Based Soft Robotic Skin Using a 3D-Printed Multi-Lattice Structure and CNN-Based Tactile Super-Resolution. This paper presents a magnet-based robotic skin that integrates a multilayer soft lattice with distributed Hall-effect sensor arrays and a tactile super-resolution model. External contact forces are converted to magnetic field changes by embedded permanent magnets, and the lattice spreads these changes across the sensing domain. This gives each sensor a large, overlapping receptive field and enables a large sensing area with minimal blind spots. Lattice parameters are tunable, enabling joint adjustment of mechanical compliance and transduction characteristics. An implicit modeling workflow and selective laser sintering (SLS) 3D printing support rapid fabrication of conformal, high-complexity structures. A convolutional neural network trained on experimental measurements estimates contact location and normal force in real time. Experiments validate localization accuracy and indicate scalability to larger surfaces, suggesting applicability to whole-body robotic skin and safe human-robot interaction.

judged.chunk_text: BactoBot: A Low-Cost, Bacteria-Inspired Soft Underwater Robot for Marine Exploration. Traditional rigid underwater vehicles pose risks to delicate marine ecosystems due to high-speed propellers and rigid hulls. This paper presents BactoBot, a low-cost, soft underwater robot designed for safe and gentle marine exploration. Inspired by the efficient flagellar propulsion of bacteria, BactoBot features 12 flexible, silicone-based arms arranged on a dodecahedral frame. Unlike high-cost research platforms, this prototype was fabricated using accessible DIY methods, including food-grade silicone molding, FDM 3D printing, and off-the-shelf DC motors. A novel multi-stage waterproofing protocol was developed to seal rotating shafts using a grease-filled chamber system, ensuring reliability at low cost. The robot was successfully tested in a controlled aquatic environment, demonstrating stable forward propulsion and turning maneuvers. With a total fabrication cost of approximately $355 USD, this project validates the feasibility of democratizing soft robotics for marine science in resource-constrained settings.

The term, a portmanteau of elastic polymer, is often used interchangeably with rubber, although the latter is preferred when referring to vulcanisates. Each of the monomers which link to form the polymer is usually a compound of several elements among carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and silicon. Rubber-like solids with elastic properties are called elastomers. Polymer chains are held together in these materials by relatively weak intermolecular bonds, which permit the polymers to stretch in response to macroscopic stresses. Elastomers are usually thermosets (requiring vulcanization) but may also be thermoplastic (see thermoplastic elastomer). The long polymer chains cross-link during curing (i.e., vulcanizing). The molecular structure of elastomers can be imagined as a 'spaghetti and meatball' structure, with the meatballs signifying cross-links. The elasticity is derived from the ability of the long chains to reconfigure themselves to distribute an applied stress.

Each of the monomers which link to form the polymer is usually a compound of several elements among carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and silicon. Rubber-like solids with elastic properties are called elastomers. Polymer chains are held together in these materials by relatively weak intermolecular bonds, which permit the polymers to stretch in response to macroscopic stresses. Elastomers are usually thermosets (requiring vulcanization) but may also be thermoplastic (see thermoplastic elastomer). The long polymer chains cross-link during curing (i.e., vulcanizing). The molecular structure of elastomers can be imagined as a 'spaghetti and meatball' structure, with the meatballs signifying cross-links. The elasticity is derived from the ability of the long chains to reconfigure themselves to distribute an applied stress.

judged.chunk_text: The elasticity is derived from the ability of the long chains to reconfigure themselves to distribute an applied stress. Unlike metals or rigid crystals where elasticity comes from changing interatomic bond distances (energy elasticity), elastomer elasticity is entropy-driven. In an unstressed state, polymer chains assume random coiled configurations (maximum entropy). Stretching forces the chains into aligned, ordered states (lower entropy). Upon releasing stress, thermal motion restores the random coiled state.

judged.chunk_text: Real-time Puncture Detection and Recovery for Pneumatic Soft Actuators. Soft robots offer safe and adaptive interaction with humans and unstructured environments through their inherent ability to deform and comply. Pneumatic actuators are one way to build soft robots. They are typically made from soft silicone materials and are especially effective for driving such systems, enabling smooth and adaptable motion. However, their compliant nature also makes them vulnerable to mechanical failures like punctures and tears, limiting practical deployment. To address this, we propose a puncture detection system for soft actuators using motion data from a single inertial measurement unit. Extracted features are used to train anomaly detectors for puncture detection and non-linear models to estimate severity. We also introduce a multi-chamber pneumatic soft bending actuator capable of diverse configurations via selective chamber inflation. Our algorithm identifies the punctured chamber and provides a severity score using a chamber perturbation scheme. Anomaly detectors are trained on normal operation data and detect damage through reconstruction errors, while severity is estimated by a separate model trained under slightly modified conditions. Finally, we demonstrate a failure recovery strategy to maintain actuation force post-failure.

judged.chunk_text: Soft Pneumatic Actuators for Soft Robotics: A Motion-Based Review of Actuation Mechanisms and Performance Trade-offs. Soft pneumatic actuators are widely used in soft robotics because they can produce large motions while remaining compliant enough to interact safely with objects, environments, and the human body. However, their performance is not solely determined by pressure. Instead, the response depends on the way the actuator is built, including the shape of its chambers, the placement of reinforcements, the use of folds, material stiffness, and the constraints that guide its deformation. As the literature has expanded, it has become more difficult to determine which mechanism is most suitable for a given application and which reported results can be compared across studies. This review examines soft pneumatic actuators according to the design strategies used to generate four motion classes: linear, bending, twisting, and omnidirectional actuation. For each class, it analyzes the structural features that define the deformation path, including braid angle, fold geometry, fiber orientation, chamber arrangement, structural asymmetry, and internal constraint layers.

judged.chunk_text: Design, Modelling and Characterisation of a Miniature Fibre-Reinforced Soft Bending Actuator for Endoluminal Interventions. Miniaturised soft pneumatic actuators are crucial for robotic intervention within highly constrained anatomical pathways. This work presents the design and validation of a fibre-reinforced soft actuator at the centimetre scale for inte- gration into an endoluminal robotic platform for natural-orifice interventional and diagnostic applications. A single-chamber geometry reinforced with embedded Kevlar fibre was de- signed to maximise curvature while preserving sealing integrity, fabricated using a multi-stage multi-stiffness silicone casting process, and validated against a high-fidelity Abaqus FEM using experimentally parametrised hyperelastic material models and embedded beam reinforcement. The semi-cylindrical actuator has an outer diameter of 18,mm and a length of 37.5,mm. Single and double helix winding configurations, fibre pitch, and fibre density were investigated.

judged.chunk_text: 3D printing, also called additive manufacturing, is the construction of a three-dimensional object from a CAD model or a digital 3D model. It can be done in a variety of processes in which material is deposited, joined or solidified under computer control, with the material being added together (e.g. plastics, liquids, or powder grains being fused), typically layer by layer. In the 1980s, 3D printing techniques were considered suitable only for the production of functional or aesthetic prototypes, and a more appropriate term for it at the time was rapid prototyping. As of 2019, the precision, repeatability, and material range of 3D printing have increased to the point that some 3D printing processes are considered viable as an industrial-production technology; in this context, the term additive manufacturing can be used synonymously with 3D printing. One of the key advantages of 3D printing is the ability to produce very complex shapes or geometries that would be otherwise infeasible to construct by hand, including hollow parts or parts with internal truss structures to reduce weight while creating less material waste. Fused deposition modeling (FDM), which uses a continuous filament of a thermoplastic material, is the most common 3D printing process in use as of 2020.

judged.chunk_text: Additive Manufacturing-Facilitated Blow Molding for Functional Thin-Walled Polymeric Structures. Thin-walled structures capable of large, reversible deformation are key to multistable structures, origami, kirigami, and soft robotics. However, conventional fabrication techniques, including 3D printing, casting, and laser cutting, suffer from poor surface quality, low durability, complex processing steps, and restricted geometric freedom, hindering the repeatable production of thin-walled, continuous structures. Here, an additive manufacturing-facilitated blow molding (AM-BM) approach is introduced, combining the design flexibility of additive manufacturing with the robustness of blow molding. By replacing metal molds with 3D-printed resin ones, AM-BM enables rapid, low-cost fabrication of thin-walled polymeric components with tunable geometry and controllable wall thickness across diverse thermoplastic materials. The thickness control allows thin-walled components to function either as rigid load-bearing elements or as compliant hinges that permit reversible deformation.

answers.answer: Soft robotics is a subfield of robotics that focuses on the design, control, and fabrication of robots made from compliant materials, as opposed to rigid components like metals, ceramics, or hard plastics [1]. These robots are typically made from flexible, elastic materials and are inspired by biological organisms such as octopuses, worms, and starfish [2]. Their compliance allows for safer interaction with humans and delicate environments, making them suitable for applications in healthcare, human-robot interaction, and tactile storytelling [1][6].

Soft robots are usually built from compliant, flexible, and elastic materials, such as elastomers, soft polymers, and other compliant materials that allow for safe and adaptive interaction with environments and humans [1]. These materials contrast with the rigid materials like metals, ceramics, and hard plastics used in traditional robotics [1]. Specific examples include materials used in soft pneumatic actuators, which rely on flexible, airtight structures that can deform under pressure [5].

Soft robots move without rigid joints by leveraging compliant materials and deformation-based actuation mechanisms. Instead of relying on traditional joints, they utilize principles such as shape change, nonlinear instability, and passive guidance. For example, snapping metabeams exploit nonlinear instability to generate rapid geometric transitions, enabling reciprocating and non-reciprocating motion in tendon-driven systems [4]. Similarly, inchworm-inspired robots use groove-guided locomotion on patterned substrates to control direction passively, eliminating the need for multiple actuators or rigid joints [6]. Magnetic actuators and dielectric elastomer actuators also enable complex motions like crawling, grasping, and propulsion through reversible deformation of soft materials [3]. These approaches demonstrate that motion in soft robotics arises from material properties and geometric design rather than rigid mechanical components.

Soft robots are used for applications that require compliance, safety in human interaction, and adaptability to complex environments. They are employed in physical rehabilitation to assist patients with neuromotor impairments, such as in upper-limb exoskeletons and soft robotic exogloves designed to improve mobility and reduce pain and spasticity in conditions like stroke or arthritis [3][4]. Their compliance allows safe interaction with humans, making them suitable for wearable devices and assistive technologies [1]. Additionally, soft robots are used in delicate manipulation tasks, such as handling fragile objects or inspecting confined spaces, due to their ability to conform to irregular shapes and provide safe, adaptive motion [6]. They also inspire bio-mimetic designs, mimicking the movement of biological organisms like octopuses, worms, and starfish [5].

Silicone rubber is made of silicone, a polymer composed of silicon, carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen [1]. It is technically known as a polysiloxane, with polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) being a common subset [2]. The material may also contain fillers to enhance properties or reduce cost [1].

Silicone rubber is typically cured through a chemical process that involves cross-linking polymer chains. This can be achieved through various methods depending on the formulation, such as addition curing, condensation curing, or peroxide curing. In addition curing, for example, a platinum catalyst is used to cross-link the polymer chains, resulting in a stable elastomer. The curing process is essential for transforming the liquid or soft silicone precursor into a solid, elastic material with the desired mechanical properties [1].
Silicone rubber can withstand temperatures from −55 to 300 °C (−70 to 570 °F) while maintaining its useful properties [1].

Silicone rubber is used for moulded parts because it is stable, non-reactive, and resistant to extreme temperatures ranging from −55 to 300 °C while maintaining its useful properties [1]. It is also easy to manufacture and shape, making it suitable for a wide variety of applications including molds for industrial, medical, and consumer products [1]. Additionally, silicone rubber is inert, non-toxic, and non-flammable, which enhances its safety and versatility in diverse environments [3]. These properties, combined with its ability to be formulated in one- or two-part systems and modified with fillers for improved performance or reduced cost, make it ideal for moulded components across multiple industries [1].

Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), also known as dimethylpolysiloxane or dimethicone, is a silicone polymer with a wide range of applications. It is optically clear, inert, non-toxic, and non-flammable, and is known for its unique rheological (flow) properties [1]. PDMS is a type of silicone oil (polymerized siloxane) used in various fields, including cosmetics, medical devices, food (as an antifoaming agent), shampoos (to make hair shiny and slippery), caulk, lubricants, and heat-resistant tiles [1]. It is also employed in soft-robotics fabrication due to its elastomeric properties and ease of processing [3].

PDMS is used for a wide range of applications due to its optical clarity, inertness, non-toxicity, and non-flammability. It is commonly used in contact lenses, medical devices, and elastomers. It is also found in shampoos to make hair shiny and slippery, in food as an antifoaming agent, in caulk, lubricants, and heat-resistant tiles [1]. Additionally, PDMS is employed in industrial lubrication and passive daytime radiative cooling [1].
Yes, PDMS is optically clear [1].

An elastomer is a type of polymer with viscoelasticity, meaning it exhibits both viscosity and elasticity, and is characterized by weak intermolecular forces, low Young's modulus, and high failure strain [1]. It is often referred to as an elastic polymer, derived from the term "elastic polymer" [6]. Elastomers can be stretched significantly and return to their original shape when the stress is removed, due to the ability of their long polymer chains to reconfigure themselves [2]. This elasticity is entropy-driven: in an unstressed state, the chains are in a random, coiled configuration (maximum entropy), and when stretched, they become more ordered (lower entropy); upon release, thermal motion restores the random configuration [2]. The molecular structure resembles a "spaghetti and meatball" model, with cross-links acting as the meatballs that prevent the chains from slipping while allowing recovery [1]. Elastomers include natural rubber, synthetic rubbers like styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), and silicone rubber [6]. They are used in applications requiring flexibility, shock absorption, electrical insulation, and resistance to extreme temperatures or environmental conditions [4].

An elastomer returns to its original shape because its long polymer chains are in a random, coiled configuration in the unstressed state, which corresponds to maximum entropy. When stretched, the chains align and become more ordered, reducing entropy. Upon release of the stress, thermal motion drives the chains back to their original random, coiled state, restoring the material to its initial shape [1]. This entropy-driven recovery is the fundamental reason for the elastic behavior of elastomers [2].

Elastomers are cross-linked during curing, a process often referred to as vulcanization [1]. This involves forming covalent bonds between polymer chains, creating a network structure that prevents the chains from slipping past one another while still allowing elasticity [3]. The cross-links act like "meatballs" in a "spaghetti and meatball" structure, holding the long chains together without restricting their ability to reconfigure under stress [1]. The degree of cross-linking is carefully balanced—enough to prevent slippage, but not so much that the chains lose their ability to return to a random, coiled state after deformation [3].

A pneumatic actuator is a device that converts energy, typically in the form of compressed air, into mechanical motion. This motion can be either linear or rotary, depending on the type of actuator [1]. In the context of soft robotics, pneumatic actuators are often made from soft silicone materials and are used to enable smooth and adaptable motion, allowing safe interaction with humans and unstructured environments [2].

Compressed air produces motion in a pneumatic actuator by converting the energy from the pressurized air into mechanical motion. When compressed air is introduced into the actuator, it exerts pressure on internal components, such as a diaphragm or piston, causing them to move. This movement can be linear or rotary, depending on the actuator's design [1].

The pressure required by a pneumatic actuator depends on several factors, including the actuator's design, size, intended motion, loading conditions, and material properties. There is no universal pressure value, as performance is influenced by structural features such as chamber geometry, reinforcement placement, fold design, and material stiffness [4]. The operating pressure must be selected based on the specific application requirements, such as force generation, motion output, and actuator size [2]. Additionally, the pneumatic supply and hysteresis characteristics also affect the necessary pressure levels [2]. Therefore, the required pressure varies across different designs and use cases.

3D printing, also known as additive manufacturing, is a process that creates three-dimensional objects by adding material layer by layer under computer control [1]. It involves constructing an object from a digital 3D model or CAD file, with materials such as plastics, liquids, or powder grains being fused or joined to form the final structure [1]. This method allows for the production of complex geometries, including hollow parts or internal structures, which are difficult or impossible to create using traditional manufacturing techniques [1]. The process is widely used in prototyping and industrial production, with fused deposition modeling (FDM) being one of the most common methods [1].

Several 3D printing methods are compatible with flexible materials, particularly those designed for elastomers or soft polymers. Fused deposition modeling (FDM), the most common 3D printing process, can work with flexible thermoplastic materials such as TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane) [2]. Additionally, rotational multi-material 3D printing has been used to fabricate soft robotic matter with elastomeric shells and fugitive cores, demonstrating the capability to print with flexible, elastomeric materials [1]. Another method, additive manufacturing-facilitated blow molding (AM-BM), uses 3D-printed resin molds to produce thin-walled polymeric structures from thermoplastic materials, enabling the creation of flexible, compliant components [5]. These approaches show that FDM, multi-material printing, and AM-BM are viable methods for working with flexible materials.

3D printing differs from moulding in that it builds objects layer by layer from a digital model using additive processes, whereas moulding typically involves shaping material by filling a pre-made mould, often through casting or injection. In 3D printing, the object is constructed directly from the ground up, enabling complex geometries, internal structures, and customization without the need for a separate mould [1]. In contrast, moulding relies on a fixed mould shape, limiting design flexibility and requiring additional tooling for each part variation [2]. Additionally, 3D printing allows for rapid prototyping and on-demand fabrication, while traditional moulding is generally more suited for mass production of identical parts [1].

Robotika lunak adalah cabang robotika yang berfokus pada perancangan dan pengembangan robot yang terbuat dari material lunak, fleksibel, dan elastis, meniru karakteristik organisme biologis seperti gurita, ulat, dan bintang laut [1]. Berbeda dengan robot konvensional yang menggunakan struktur kaku, robotika lunak menggunakan material yang dapat berubah bentuk dan menyesuaikan diri dengan lingkungan, sehingga meningkatkan keamanan saat beroperasi dekat manusia [2]. Material lunak ini memungkinkan robot untuk menunjukkan fleksibilitas dan adaptasi yang tinggi, yang bermanfaat dalam aplikasi seperti medis dan manufaktur [6].

Material yang biasanya digunakan untuk membuat robot lunak adalah elastomer, yaitu polimer yang fleksibel dan elastis seperti karet alam, karet sintetik (misalnya butadiene rubber/SBR), dan karet silikon [2]. Elastomer mampu kembali ke bentuk semula setelah direntangkan, sehingga cocok untuk aplikasi robot lunak yang membutuhkan fleksibilitas dan deformasi [2]. Selain elastomer, robot lunak juga dapat dibuat menggunakan material lain yang komplian, seperti bahan yang digunakan dalam pencetakan 3D dengan teknik FDM atau stereolitografi [4].

Robot lunak dapat bergerak tanpa sendi kaku dengan memanfaatkan perubahan bentuk dan deformasi dari material lunak yang fleksibel, seperti elastomer atau bahan berbasis polimer. Gerakan ini dihasilkan melalui berbagai mekanisme, seperti kontraksi otot buatan, perubahan geometri struktur, atau transisi geometris cepat akibat ketidakstabilan nonlinier. Misalnya, sistem berbasis tendon dapat menggerakkan sirip robot lunak dengan dua mode: gerak bolak-balik (reciprocating) dan gerak non-bolak-balik (non-reciprocating), yang dihasilkan dari struktur snapping metabeams berbentuk spiral yang dapat berubah bentuk secara cepat dan reversibel [2]. Selain itu, robot dengan bentuk spiral logaritmik dapat dikendalikan secara tertutup melalui kontrol berbasis Jacobian yang memperhitungkan deformasi nonlinier dan ketidaksesuaian geometri, memungkinkan gerakan kompleks tanpa sendi kaku [4]. Dengan demikian, gerakan robot lunak didorong oleh deformasi material dan desain geometri, bukan oleh sendi mekanik kaku.

Robot lunak digunakan untuk meniru karakteristik organisme biologis seperti gurita, ulat, dan bintang laut, yang memungkinkan mereka bergerak fleksibel dan menyesuaikan diri dengan lingkungan secara dinamis [1]. Mereka cocok untuk tugas-tugas yang membutuhkan adaptasi bentuk, seperti penjelajahan medan kasar, manipulasi objek lembut, atau interaksi aman dengan manusia, karena material lunaknya aman dan dapat menyesuaikan deformasi tanpa merusak [5]. Selain itu, robot lunak juga digunakan dalam aplikasi seperti kontrol tertutup berbasis morfologi spesifik, misalnya pada lengan kontinuum berbentuk spiral logaritmik yang mampu menangkap dan meraih objek dengan presisi [4].

Karet silikon terbuat dari polimer silikon yang mengandung karbon, hidrogen, dan oksigen, yang dikenal sebagai getah silikone atau polidimetilsiloksan (PDMS) [3]. Getah silikone merupakan elastomer yang bersifat stabil, tidak reaktif, dan tahan terhadap suhu ekstrem dari −55 hingga 300 °C, sehingga cocok untuk berbagai aplikasi industri [2][6]. Sifat-sifat ini membuat karet silikon ideal untuk digunakan dalam bidang seperti elektronik, otomotif, kesehatan, dan makanan [2][6].

Sumber yang diberikan tidak menjelaskan proses pengeringan karet silikon secara khusus. Namun, dari informasi yang tersedia, dapat diketahui bahwa karet silikon (silicone rubber) adalah elastomer yang umumnya stabil dan tahan terhadap suhu ekstrem, serta dapat dibentuk dan diproses dengan mudah [1]. Proses pengeringan atau pengerasan (curing) karet silikon biasanya melibatkan reaksi kimia seperti pembentukan silil-oksida (siloxane) yang terjadi pada suhu tertentu atau dengan katalis, tergantung pada formulasi (misalnya, satu bagian atau dua bagian) [6]. Namun, detail proses pengeringan tidak disebutkan dalam sumber yang tersedia.

Jadi, berdasarkan sumber yang diberikan, tidak ada informasi yang cukup untuk menjelaskan bagaimana karet silikon dikeringkan.
Karet silikon dapat menahan suhu berjulat dari −55 hingga 300 °C [1].

Karet silikon digunakan untuk bagian cetakan karena memiliki sifat yang stabil, tahan terhadap suhu ekstrem (dari −55 hingga 300 °C), serta tidak reaktif dan mudah dibentuk [2]. Selain itu, elastomer berbasis silikon seperti polidimetilsiloksan (PDMS) bersifat inert, tidak beracun, dan transparan secara optik, sehingga cocok untuk aplikasi yang membutuhkan kebersihan dan ketahanan terhadap kondisi keras [4]. Sifat elastis dan fleksibelnya memungkinkan karet silikon digunakan untuk mencetak bentuk kompleks tanpa kerusakan, serta mudah dilepaskan dari cetakan [5].

Polidimetilsiloksan (PDMS), juga dikenal sebagai dimetilpolisiloksan atau dimetikon, adalah polimer silikona yang bersifat optik bening, umumnya inert, tidak beracun, dan tidak mudah terbakar [1]. PDMS dikenal karena sifat reologi (aliran) yang tidak biasa dan digunakan dalam berbagai aplikasi, mulai dari lensa kontak dan alat kesehatan hingga elastomer, sampo, makanan (sebagai agen pengawabusa), pelumas, dan ubin tahan panas [1]. PDMS merupakan salah satu jenis minyak silikon atau siloksan terpolimerisasi [1].

PDMS (Polidimetilsiloksan) digunakan dalam berbagai aplikasi seperti lensa kontak, alat kesehatan, elastomer, sampo (sebagai agen membuat rambut berkilau), makanan (sebagai agen pengawet), pakal, pelumas, dan ubin tahan panas [1]. PDMS juga digunakan dalam industri untuk pelumasan, pendinginan radiasi pasif di siang hari, serta sebagai bahan dalam pencetakan 3D dan perangkat lunak robot lunak [2][3].
Ya, PDMS transparan [1].

Elastomer adalah polimer yang memiliki sifat elastis, artinya dapat diregangkan hingga panjang yang jauh melebihi ukuran awalnya dan kembali ke bentuk semula ketika gaya ditarik dilepaskan. Sifat ini disebabkan oleh intermolekul yang lemah dan adanya ikatan silang yang memadai pada rantai panjang polimer, sehingga molekul dapat kembali ke susunan acak setelah diregangkan [1]. Elastomer juga dikenal sebagai "elastic polymer" dan merupakan bahan seperti karet yang fleksibel dan elastis [2]. Mereka biasanya bersifat viskoelastis, memiliki modulus Young yang rendah dan daya regang yang tinggi dibandingkan material lain [4]. Contoh elastomer meliputi karet alam, karet sintetik seperti stirena-butadiena, serta getah silikon [2].

Elastomer kembali ke bentuk semula kerana molekulnya berada dalam susunan yang acak (rawak) pada keadaan tidak tertarik, yang merupakan keadaan dengan entropi maksimum [3]. Ketika elastomer direntangkan, rantai polimer terpaksa berbaris secara teratur, mengurangi entropi [3]. Apabila gaya dilepaskan, gerakan termal secara spontan mengembalikan rantai polimer ke susunan acak, sehingga elastomer kembali ke bentuk asalnya [2]. Proses ini didorong oleh perubahan entropi, bukan oleh gaya ikatan antaratom seperti pada logam [3]. Selain itu, ikatan silang yang minimal memastikan rantai tidak tergelincir, namun masih membolehkan perubahan bentuk balik [1].

Elastomer saling mengikat melalui ikatan silang (cross-links) antar rantai polimer. Ikatan silang ini cukup sedikit untuk memastikan rantai-rantai polimer tidak tergelincir satu sama lain, namun tidak terlalu banyak sehingga membatasi kemampuan rantai untuk kembali ke bentuk awal setelah ditarik [1]. Ikatan silang ini membantu menjaga struktur elastomer tetap stabil saat diregangkan, namun tetap memungkinkan molekul kembali ke susunan acak (rawak) secara spontan saat gaya dilepaskan [1]. Struktur ini sering digambarkan seperti "spaghetti dan meatball", di mana "meatball" mewakili titik-titik silang yang menghubungkan rantai panjang [4].

Aktuator pneumatik adalah perangkat yang mengubah energi (biasanya dalam bentuk udara terkompresi) menjadi gerakan mekanis, yang dapat berupa gerakan putar atau linier, tergantung pada jenis aktuator tersebut [3]. Dalam konteks robotik lunak, aktuator pneumatik umumnya terbuat dari bahan silikon lunak dan digunakan untuk menghasilkan gerakan halus serta adaptif, memungkinkan interaksi yang aman dengan manusia dan lingkungan yang tidak terstruktur [1].

Udara terkompresi menghasilkan gerakan pada aktuator dengan mengubah energi menjadi gerak mekanis. Dalam aktuator pneumatik, tekanan udara yang diterapkan ke dalam ruang tertutup menyebabkan perubahan bentuk atau perpindahan pada bagian aktuator, seperti piston atau membran, yang menghasilkan gerakan linier atau rotari [1].

Tekanan yang dibutuhkan oleh aktuator pneumatik tidak ditentukan secara spesifik dalam sumber yang tersedia. Namun, beberapa sumber menyebutkan bahwa aktuator dapat beroperasi hingga tekanan tertentu, misalnya pada sumber [2], aktuator dapat mempertahankan kekuatan struktural hingga 100 kPa. Tekanan operasional aktual bergantung pada desain, bahan, dan aplikasi, seperti yang disebutkan dalam sumber [5] dan [6], yang menekankan bahwa kinerja aktuator dipengaruhi oleh berbagai faktor desain, termasuk bentuk kamar, penempatan penguat, dan kondisi beban. Oleh karena itu, tekanan yang dibutuhkan harus ditentukan berdasarkan desain spesifik dan kebutuhan aplikasi.

Pencetakan 3D adalah proses mencipta objek tiga dimensi dengan menambahkan bahan secara lapis demi lapis di bawah kawalan komputer, menggunakan data model digital seperti dari model 3D atau fail AMF [1]. Teknik ini juga dikenali sebagai additive manufacturing (AM) atau pembuatan tambahan, di mana bahan seperti plastik, cecair, atau serbuk diproses secara berturut-turut untuk membentuk objek akhir [2][4]. Pencetakan 3D membolehkan hasil bentuk yang kompleks, termasuk struktur dalaman seperti truss atau bahagian berongga, yang sukar dicapai dengan kaedah pembuatan tradisional [4].

Beberapa metode pencetakan 3D yang dapat bekerja dengan bahan fleksibel, seperti elastomer atau plastik fleksibel, antara lain:

- **Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM)**: Metode ini menggunakan filament termoplastik yang dilelehkan dan ditembakkan lapis demi lapis. Dengan penggunaan material termoplastik fleksibel seperti TPU (Thermoplastic Polyurethane), FDM dapat memproses bahan fleksibel secara efektif [3].  
- **Stereolitografi (SLA)**: Metode ini menggunakan cairan fotopolimer yang diproses dengan sinar laser untuk membentuk lapisan demi lapisan. Bahan fotopolimer fleksibel tersedia secara khusus untuk SLA, memungkinkan pencetakan struktur elastis atau fleksibel [1][2].  
- **Multimaterial 3D Printing**: Teknik ini memungkinkan pencetakan dengan lebih dari satu jenis material dalam satu proses, termasuk material fleksibel dan kaku secara bersamaan. Pendekatan ini digunakan dalam pengembangan robot lunak, di mana distribusi material dan geometri struktur dioptimalkan secara bersamaan [4].  

Metode-metode ini mendukung pencetakan bahan fleksibel seperti elastomer, yang digunakan untuk aplikasi seperti penyerap getaran, pelindung, atau komponen robot lunak [5].

Referensi: [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]
